contributions.headingText: Myeloid neoplasms involving the skin are composed of myeloid cells/blasts with or without maturation. Myeloid neoplasms involving skin can form a tumour that effaces architecture (i.e. myeloid sarcoma [MS] regardless of blast percentage), or they can infiltrate skin without architectural effacement. For non–tumour-forming myeloid neoplasms in skin with blasts ≥ 20%, the diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) involving skin is most appropriate.

Acceptable: leukaemia cutis.

Not recommended: granulocytic or monocytic sarcoma; extramedullary myeloid tumour; chloroma.

The skin is a frequent location of myeloid neoplasms, particularly MS, which occurs in 20–30% of all cases of AML {17170724; 28574302; 29532520; 31866570; 31682773}. The trunk, extremities, and head/neck are the most common sites of involvement {18089498; 23165700; 21228369; 24274424; 28296991; 31866570; 34788403}.

Myeloid neoplasms may manifest as skin lesions in patients with or without a history of AML, myelodysplastic neoplasm (MDS), myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN), or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm (MDS/MPN) including chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML).

MS can occur concomitantly or after the onset of AML or (less often) other myeloid neoplasms in blood and/or bone marrow; occasionally (~10%) MS can precede AML {18089498; 21228369; 23165700}. Cutaneous involvement by other myeloid neoplasms is less common {22895265; 28296991; 31866570}. A small subset of patients with MDS have a skin lesion and clinical manifestations of the recently described VEXAS (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic) syndrome with associated mutation in UBA1 {33108101; 34788403}.

Patients may have single or multiple skin lesions, manifesting as violaceous or haemorrhagic papules, plaques, nodules, or blueberry muffin lesions (in infants) {8215495; 18089498; 22895265; 23165700; 21228369; 24274424; 31866570}.

The prevalence of cutaneous myeloid infiltrates in patients with myeloid neoplasms ranges from 1% to 10–20% depending on the underlying myeloid neoplasm and is higher in cases of AML with monocytic differentiation. MS occurs in 3–10% of patients with AML and affects children and adults, with most cases involving adults aged > 50 years, with a male predominance {11907789; 18089498; 23165700; 31682773}. The prevalence of MS may be higher (20–30%) in infants with congenital myeloid leukaemia {8215495}.

The etiology of cutaneous myeloid neoplasms is similar to that of their equivalent neoplasms in blood and bone marrow. The molecular mechanisms responsible for skin tropism are not well defined, but adhesion molecules, chemokine receptor–ligand interactions, and extracellular matrix interactions may have an important role {20582977; 32033262}.

Cutaneous myeloid neoplasms share cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities with systemic myeloid neoplasms {23190893; 31866570; 33213985; 33232718; 34788403; 35201334}. Shared abnormalities in MS with AML (concordant in 60–80% of cases) include monosomy 7, trisomy 8, abnormalities of 11q23/KMT2A, and gene mutations in NPM1, FLT3, and the RAS pathway (e.g. PTPN11) {31866570; 17170724; 23165700; 17443224; 26113416; 33213985; 33232718}. NPM1 is the most commonly mutated gene in cutaneous MS with associated monocytic differentiation {17443224; 26113416; 31866570}.
MS has a fish-flesh cut surface and may appear green in neoplasms with granulocytic differentiation because the cells express myeloperoxidase.

Myeloid neoplasms with architectural effacement of skin: Cutaneous MS forms a tumour that effaces normal skin architecture. Immature myeloid cells are arranged in diffuse sheets in the dermis and/or subcutaneous tissue, with sparing of the epidermis (grenz zone). The neoplastic cells are of medium-large size and have thin nuclear membranes, fine (blastic) chromatin, and (usually) pinpoint nucleoli. Tumours with monocytic differentiation include cells with folded nuclei (e.g. promonocytes). Tumours with granulocytic differentiation often show a subset of immature neoplastic cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm.

Myeloid neoplasms without architectural effacement of skin: Myeloid neoplasms can infiltrate skin in a perivascular, periadnexal, patchy nodular, or interstitial infiltrate involving the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Myeloid neoplasms with this pattern of infiltration include AML, CMML, MDS, and MDS/MPN {18089498; 21228369; 23165700}. Importantly, for this pattern of infiltrate with blasts ≥ 20%, the diagnosis of AML involving skin is most appropriate. The infiltrate in CMML may be accompanied by plasmacytoid dendritic cells, either scattered individually or forming nodules {22895265}. The infiltrate in MDS and other myeloid neoplasms can consist of predominantly mature neutrophils (as in classic Sweet syndrome) or immature/maturing myelomonocytic cells with histiocytoid morphology (histiocytoid Sweet syndrome) {28296991; 34788403; 35201334}.

Immunophenotype (immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry)

The immunophenotypic profile in myeloid neoplasms is variable given the broad spectrum of myeloid lineage differentiation (monocytic vs granulocytic) and maturation (blasts vs maturing myeloid cells) {17170724; 26185307}. The neoplastic cells generally express CD13, CD33, CD43, CD68, and myeloperoxidase (~90%). Additionally, myeloid neoplasms with monocytic differentiation often express CD4, CD11c, CD14 (variable), CD56 (~50%), lysozyme, and abnormal cytoplasmic NPM1 (~40% in MS, indicative of NPM1 mutation), but they often lack CD34 and KIT (CD117), whereas immature myeloid infiltrate with granulocytic differentiation may express CD34 and KIT (CD117) {17170724; 17443224; 23165700; 26113416; 28574302}.

Differential diagnosis

Myeloid infiltrates with a predominance of blasts (such as MS) should be distinguished from blastic plasmacytoid dendritic neoplasm and large cell lymphomas. Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm is positive for CD4, CD56, CD123, CD303, TCL1, and TCF4, but lacks myeloperoxidase or lysozyme {24390220; 31261288}. Large cell lymphomas are positive for lymphoid markers, such as CD3, CD19, and CD20.

Myeloid neoplasms with a predominance of maturing or mature myelomonocytic cells and lacking architecture effacement or a high blast count need to be distinguished from inflammatory dermatoses.
Wright–Giemsa touch imprints or smears highlight large neoplastic cells with cytoplasmic granules {31051716}.

No specific molecular or cytogenetic tests are required to establish a diagnosis of cutaneous involvement by myeloid neoplasms. MS is considered clinically to be equivalent to AML {26185307; 32577912}. Comprehensive evaluation that includes cytogenetic analysis and molecular assessment for translocations and gene mutations is needed for correct classification and for planning therapy.

Essential for myeloid sarcoma: effacement of normal skin architecture by a tumour composed of myeloid blasts, with or without maturing elements, positive for granulocytic and/or monocytic markers.

Essential for other myeloid neoplasms: in the absence of architectural effacement of skin, a descriptive diagnosis of cutaneous involvement by a neoplastic myeloid infiltrate is preferred; for this pattern of myeloid infiltrate with blasts ≥ 20%, the diagnosis of AML involving skin is most appropriate.

Evaluation of blood and bone marrow for AML or other myeloid neoplasms (e.g. MDS, MPN, MDS/MPN) is mandatory. The prognosis is largely dictated by the genetics of the underlying myeloid neoplasms. Cutaneous myeloid infiltrates in patients with MDS seem to be associated with MDS progression and a poorer prognosis {34788403}. The recommended therapy by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) for patients with MS is AML-type chemotherapy. The prognosis is similar to that of AML without evidence of MS {23165700; 32577912}. Patients with isolated MS appear to have a better prognosis than patients with concomitant AML involving bone marrow {25213180; 34346084; 34380367}.
